provenance: Acquired circa late 1970sThence by descent Sir David Orr (1922 â 2008) was a businessman and philanthropist known for his leadership of multinational corporations. Orr was born near Dublin and enlisted in the Royal Engineers during WWII at age 19. He served in Burma with Queen Victoriaâs Own Madras Sappers and Miners, a prestigious regiment of the British Indian Army, where he earned two Military Crosses for his bravery. Orr joined the multinational company Unilever in 1948 as a graduate trainee, following the completion of his law degree at Trinity College, Dublin.  In 1955, Orr was posted to India, where he served as marketing director for Hindustan Lever, later rising to vice-chairman of the Lever Brothers India in 1957. After decades at the company in various executive roles in London and New York, Orr was appointed chairman of Unilever from 1974 to 1982, overseeing the success of some of the most famous brands, including Persil, Jif, Dove, Vaseline, and Lipton. Even in retirement, Orr continued to enjoy a professional connection to South Asia as chairman of the British Council from 1985 to 1992 and the Charles Wallace Trust from 1991 to 1998.

Peter (1922 - 2002) and Lilly Glucksmann were both children when they were forced to flee Hitler's Germany. Peter emigrated to London in 1938, together with his family, while Lilly arrived alone at Liverpool Street station on one of the very last Kinder Transports in August 1939. The two met at a school for German Jewish refugees in Haslemere, Surrey, married in their early twenties, and began collecting art in the late 1950s.  As a young couple building new lives and raising a family, they spent whatever they could spare on buying art. Profoundly affected by the loss of their homes, language, and culture, they believed that a house full of paintings, sculpture, and music would gift their two young daughters something that could never be taken away from them: an appreciation of the arts. Peter was involved in fabric design and the clothing trade, befriending fashion designers such as Mary Quant in the 60s, traveling all over the world in search of textiles, and starting to buy paintings from Parisian artists who relied on fabric designs to earn money. Lilly was a teacher who ran a school for children in hospital. Throughout their lives, Peter and Lilly visited galleries in London and abroad, made many friends in the art world, and accumulated an eclectic collection of works by artists such as Marc Chagall, Armand Guillaumin, MoÃ¯se Kisling, Auguste Rodin and Souza. An active supporter of emerging talent for decades, Peter later became a trustee of the Camden Art Centre.

Vinodini and Satyapal Mayor moved to Baroda in the 1950s. Vinodini, a professor of Mathematics at the MS University of Baroda, and Satyapal, who worked at Satyadev Chemicals, were well-connected to the city's social and contemporary art scene. In the 1960s, Vinodini established what would become the famous Artist's Colony behind their home, Kamal Cottage, in the grounds of the Shiv Mahal Palace. The colony hosted a number of young artists from the 1960s through the early 1990s, including Gulammohammed Sheikh, Vivan Sundaram, and Jyoti Bhatt. Bhupen Khakhar, one of the colonyâs most famous residents, spent a decade living and working from there. Bhupen and the Mayors became great friends, and the artist would often frequent their residence at Kamal Cottage.

George M. Butcher was a prominent art critic for The Guardian and a stalwart supporter of the burgeoning South Asian modern art scene. He spent more than two years in India and befriended many artists, gallerists and art critics. Using his knowledge and contacts, he curated several important shows on the regionâs art featuring artists such as Ram Kumar, Francis Newton Souza and Anwar Jalal Shemza. Butcher was among the first writers to assert the remarkable contributions of South Asian modern artists to global modernism and left an indelible mark on South Asian art history.
